title: Parametric equations
scope: Plane curves given by parametric equations: sketching, orientation, eliminating the parameter, standard parametrizations and the cycloid, slopes and tangent lines, second derivatives and concavity, area, arc length, speed and surface area for parametric curves; polar coordinates are the next topic and vector-valued functions belong to Calculus III.

kps.d: Define parametric equations and curves, plot them from a table, and describe the orientation and motion.
Convert parametric equations to an equation in x and y and state the restrictions the parametrization imposes.
Parametrize segments, circles, ellipses and graphs with a prescribed direction, and derive the cycloid equations.
Derive and apply dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) to find tangent lines, with its hypothesis.
Locate horizontal and vertical tangents, self-intersections with several tangents, and analyse points where both derivatives vanish.
Compute d2y/dx2 correctly for a parametric curve and determine concavity.
Compute areas under parametric curves and inside simple closed curves, handling orientation and sign.
Compute arc length and speed of parametric curves, and explain the traced-once hypothesis.
Compute the area of a surface generated by rotating a parametric curve about the x-axis.

intro:
Up to now a curve in the plane has been the graph of a function \(y = f(x)\), or at most the solution set of an equation in \(x\) and \(y\). Neither description records how a curve is traced. The path of a projectile, of a planet, or of a point on a rolling wheel is determined by where the moving point is at each instant, and many such paths are not graphs of functions at all: a circle fails the vertical line test, a cycloid has sharp points, and a path may cross itself. Even when the path is a graph, the graph forgets the timing.

Parametric equations describe a curve by giving both coordinates as functions of a third variable, the parameter. This chapter develops that description and then redoes, for parametric curves, the calculus already known for graphs: slopes of tangent lines, concavity, area, arc length and surface area. Each new formula comes from the chain rule or from a substitution in a formula already known for graphs.

sections.title: Parametric equations and their curves
sections.md:
This section introduces the description of a curve by two coordinate functions of a common variable, and shows how to read such a description: plotting points, determining the direction of motion, and recovering an equation in \(x\) and \(y\) when one exists.

> **Definition.** Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions defined on an interval \(I\). The equations \(x = f(t)\), \(y = g(t)\) are **parametric equations**, the variable \(t\) is the **parameter**, and the set of points \((f(t), g(t))\) for \(t \in I\) is a **parametric curve** (or plane curve). If \(I = [a, b]\), the points \((f(a), g(a))\) and \((f(b), g(b))\) are the **initial point** and **terminal point**.

It is often helpful to think of \(t\) as time and of \((x, y)\) as the position of a moving point. The direction in which the point moves as \(t\) increases is the **orientation** of the curve, indicated on sketches by arrows.

**Worked example 1.** Sketch \(x = t^2 - 1\), \(y = t + 1\) for \(-2 \le t \le 2\). A table of values gives

| \(t\) | \(-2\) | \(-1\) | 0 | 1 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \((x, y)\) | \((3, -1)\) | \((0, 0)\) | \((-1, 1)\) | \((0, 2)\) | \((3, 3)\) |

The point starts at \((3, -1)\), moves left to the vertex \((-1, 1)\), and returns right to \((3, 3)\), always moving upward, since \(y = t + 1\) increases. To find an equation, **eliminate the parameter**: from the second equation \(t = y - 1\), and substituting gives \(x = (y-1)^2 - 1\), a parabola opening to the right. The parametric curve is the part of this parabola with \(-1 \le y \le 3\). In the graph, drag the slider \(t\) and watch the point travel along the curve in the direction of increasing \(t\).

```plot
x: -2, 4
y: -2, 4
t: -2, 2
slider: a, -2, 2, -1 | t
param: t^2 - 1; t + 1 | x = t² − 1, y = t + 1, −2 ≤ t ≤ 2
point: a^2 - 1, a + 1
```

**Worked example 2 (the circle).** For \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), the identity \(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1\) eliminates the parameter: \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\). The point starts at \((1, 0)\) and moves counterclockwise once around the unit circle. The equations \(x = \cos 2t\), \(y = \sin 2t\) on the same interval trace the same circle twice, twice as fast; \(x = \sin t\), \(y = \cos t\) trace it clockwise from \((0, 1)\). One set of points thus admits many parametrizations; the parametrization carries extra information (starting point, direction, speed, number of traversals) that the equation \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\) does not.

**Restrictions survive elimination.** For \(x = \sqrt t\), \(y = t\), \(t \ge 0\), squaring gives \(y = x^2\); but \(x = \sqrt t \ge 0\), so the curve is only the right half of the parabola. For \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin^2 t\), the identity gives \(y = 1 - x^2\) with \(-1 \le x \le 1\): the point oscillates back and forth along an arc of a parabola and never leaves it.

**Common mistakes.** Reporting the whole graph of the eliminated equation when the parametrization covers only part of it. Treating \(t\) as if it were \(x\): the parameter is a third variable, and \(t = 1\) does not mean \(x = 1\). And discarding orientation, which later matters for areas and for arc lengths.

questions.prompt: Eliminate the parameter from \(x = 2t - 1\), \(y = t^2 + 3\) and give \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
questions.why: From \(x = 2t - 1\), \(t = \frac{x+1}{2}\). Then \(y = \left(\frac{x+1}{2}\right)^2 + 3 = \frac{(x+1)^2}{4} + 3\). Since \(t\) ranges over all reals, so does \(x\), and the curve is the whole parabola.

questions.prompt: Eliminate the parameter from \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin^2 t\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Describe precisely which part of the resulting graph is traced, and how the point moves as \(t\) increases from 0 to \(2\pi\).
rubric: Uses \(\sin^2 t = 1 - \cos^2 t\) to get \(y = 1 - x^2\).
States the restriction \(-1 \le x \le 1\) (so \(0 \le y \le 1\)): only the arc of the parabola between \((-1, 0)\) and \((1, 0)\).
Describes the motion: from \((1, 0)\) at \(t = 0\) through \((0, 1)\) to \((-1, 0)\) at \(t = \pi\), then back to \((1, 0)\) at \(t = 2\pi\).
Notes the motion repeats with period \(2\pi\), so the arc is traced back and forth infinitely often.
questions.model: Since \(\sin^2 t = 1 - \cos^2 t\), every point satisfies \(y = 1 - x^2\). But \(x = \cos t\) only takes values in \([-1, 1]\), so the curve is the arc of the parabola \(y = 1 - x^2\) with \(-1 \le x \le 1\), from \((-1, 0)\) up to \((0, 1)\) and down to \((1, 0)\). At \(t = 0\) the point is at \((1, 0)\); as \(t\) increases to \(\pi\), \(x = \cos t\) decreases to \(-1\), so the point moves along the arc through \((0, 1)\) (at \(t = \frac\pi2\)) to \((-1, 0)\). As \(t\) goes from \(\pi\) to \(2\pi\), \(x\) increases back to 1 and the point retraces the arc to \((1, 0)\). Because both coordinates have period \(2\pi\), this back-and-forth motion repeats forever.
questions.why: Elimination gives the set of points only up to restrictions; the range of each coordinate function must be checked separately.

questions.prompt: A particle moves along \(x = 2 - t\), \(y = t^2 - 4t\), \(0 \le t \le 4\). Give its initial and terminal points and the direction of motion, identify the curve by eliminating the parameter, and find the point of the path with the smallest \(y\)-coordinate together with the time at which it is reached.
rubric: Initial point \((2, 0)\) at \(t = 0\), terminal point \((-2, 0)\) at \(t = 4\).
Direction: \(x = 2 - t\) decreases, so the particle moves from right to left.
Eliminates \(t = 2 - x\) to get \(y = x^2 - 4\), restricted to \(-2 \le x \le 2\).
Lowest point \((0, -4)\), reached at \(t = 2\).
questions.model: At \(t = 0\) the particle is at \((2, 0)\) and at \(t = 4\) at \((-2, 0)\). Since \(x = 2 - t\) decreases throughout, it moves from right to left. From \(t = 2 - x\), \(y = (2 - x)^2 - 4(2 - x) = x^2 - 4\); as \(t\) runs over \([0, 4]\), \(x\) runs over \([-2, 2]\), so the path is the arc of the parabola \(y = x^2 - 4\) with \(-2 \le x \le 2\), traced from right to left. The smallest value of \(y = t^2 - 4t = (t-2)^2 - 4\) is \(-4\), at \(t = 2\), where the particle is at \((0, -4)\), the vertex.
questions.why: The parametrization adds timing and direction to the parabola: the vertex is reached halfway through the motion.

sections.title: Parametrizing lines, circles and the cycloid
sections.md:
To apply calculus to a path we first need parametric equations for it. This section gives the standard parametrizations of lines, circles and ellipses, and derives the equations of the cycloid, a curve that is naturally described by a parameter and has no convenient equation in \(x\) and \(y\).

**Graphs.** Any graph \(y = F(x)\), \(a \le x \le b\), is a parametric curve with \(x = t\), \(y = F(t)\), \(a \le t \le b\). Everything proved below for parametric curves therefore includes graphs as a special case.

**Line segments.** The segment from \(P_0 = (x_0, y_0)\) to \(P_1 = (x_1, y_1)\) is
\[ x = x_0 + t(x_1 - x_0), \qquad y = y_0 + t(y_1 - y_0), \qquad 0 \le t \le 1. \]
At \(t = 0\) the point is \(P_0\), at \(t = 1\) it is \(P_1\), and at \(t = \frac12\) it is the midpoint; allowing all real \(t\) gives the whole line. For instance, the segment from \((1, -2)\) to \((4, 7)\) is \(x = 1 + 3t\), \(y = -2 + 9t\), \(0 \le t \le 1\).

**Circles and ellipses.** The circle with centre \((h, k)\) and radius \(r\) is \(x = h + r\cos t\), \(y = k + r\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), traced once counterclockwise from \((h + r, k)\); replacing \(\sin t\) by \(-\sin t\) reverses the direction. More generally \(x = h + a\cos t\), \(y = k + b\sin t\) traces the ellipse \(\frac{(x-h)^2}{a^2} + \frac{(y-k)^2}{b^2} = 1\).

**The cycloid.** A wheel of radius \(r\) rolls without slipping along the \(x\)-axis, and \(P\) is a point on its rim that starts at the origin. The **cycloid** is the path of \(P\). Use as parameter the angle \(t\) (in radians) through which the wheel has turned.

- Rolling without slipping means that the distance travelled along the ground equals the arc of rim that has touched it, \(rt\). So the centre is at \((rt, r)\).
- At the start \(P\) is directly below the centre. After a turn through \(t\) (clockwise, as the wheel rolls to the right), \(P\) is displaced from the centre by \(-r\sin t\) horizontally and \(-r\cos t\) vertically.

Adding these,
\[ x = r(t - \sin t), \qquad y = r(1 - \cos t). \]
The point touches the ground (\(y = 0\)) exactly when \(\cos t = 1\), that is, at \(t = 2\pi k\), where the curve has sharp points called **cusps**; it reaches its greatest height \(2r\) at \(t = \pi\). In the graph (\(r = 1\)), drag the rolling angle and watch the end of the spoke, the marked point on the rim, trace the cycloid; notice that the point is momentarily at rest at each cusp.

```plot
x: -0.5, 13
y: -1, 6.94
t: 0, 12.566
slider: a, 0, 12.566, 2 | rolling angle t
param: t - sin(t); 1 - cos(t) | cycloid, r = 1
param: a + cos(t); 1 + sin(t) | wheel
param: a - sin(a)*t/12.566; 1 - cos(a)*t/12.566 | spoke to the marked rim point
point: a, 1
```

Eliminating \(t\) from the cycloid equations is possible in principle (\(t = \arccos\left(1 - \frac yr\right)\) on the first half-arch) but produces an unwieldy formula, and it does not give \(y\) as a function of \(x\) across a cusp in any useful way. The parametric form is the natural one, and the next sections compute slopes, areas and lengths for the cycloid directly from it.

**Common mistakes.** Parametrizing a segment in the wrong direction or with \(t\) running over the wrong interval. Writing \(x = r\cos t\) for a circle not centred at the origin. And, for the cycloid, placing the rim point relative to the origin rather than relative to the moving centre.

questions.prompt: Give parametric equations, with the parameter interval, for (a) the line segment from \((-2, 5)\) to \((4, 1)\), traced from the first point to the second; (b) the ellipse \(\frac{(x-2)^2}{9} + \frac{(y+1)^2}{4} = 1\), traced once counterclockwise; (c) the circle of radius 3 centred at \((0, 0)\), traced once clockwise starting at \((3, 0)\). In each case, check the starting point or the direction of travel.
rubric: (a) \(x = -2 + 6t\), \(y = 5 - 4t\), \(0 \le t \le 1\) (or an equivalent parametrization with correct endpoints and direction).
Checks at least one point or direction in each case.
questions.model: (a) With \(P_0 = (-2, 5)\), \(P_1 = (4, 1)\): \(x = -2 + 6t\), \(y = 5 - 4t\), \(0 \le t \le 1\); \(t = 0\) gives \((-2, 5)\), \(t = 1\) gives \((4, 1)\). (b) Centre \((2, -1)\), semi-axes 3 and 2: \(x = 2 + 3\cos t\), \(y = -1 + 2\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\); at \(t = 0\) the point is \((5, -1)\) and \(y\) increases first, so the motion is counterclockwise. (c) \(x = 3\cos t\), \(y = -3\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\): it starts at \((3, 0)\) and \(y\) becomes negative first, so the motion is clockwise.
questions.why: Substituting into the equation of the curve verifies the set; checking the first moments of motion verifies the direction.

questions.prompt: A wheel of radius 2 rolls without slipping along the \(x\)-axis, and a point on its rim starts at the origin. How far has the centre of the wheel moved horizontally when the point first returns to the ground? Give the exact value.
questions.why: The point is on the ground when \(y = 2(1 - \cos t) = 0\), first again at \(t = 2\pi\). The centre is at \((2t, 2)\), so it has moved \(2\cdot2\pi = 4\pi\): one circumference, as rolling without slipping requires.

sections.title: Slopes and tangent lines
sections.md:
The first calculus question about a curve is its slope. For a parametric curve the slope \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) must be obtained from the two rates \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt}\); this section derives the formula, uses it to find tangent lines and points where the tangent is horizontal or vertical, and examines what happens when both rates vanish.

> **Theorem (slope of a parametric curve).** Let \(x = x(t)\), \(y = y(t)\) have continuous first derivatives, and suppose \(x'(t_0) \ne 0\). Then near \(t_0\) the curve is the graph of a differentiable function of \(x\), and at the point corresponding to \(t_0\)
> \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{y'(t_0)}{x'(t_0)}. \]

*Why.* Since \(x'\) is continuous and \(x'(t_0) \ne 0\), \(x'\) keeps one sign near \(t_0\), so \(x\) is strictly monotone in \(t\) there; hence \(t\) is a function of \(x\) and \(y\) becomes a function of \(x\). Differentiating \(y(t) = F(x(t))\) by the chain rule gives \(y'(t) = F'(x(t))\,x'(t)\), and solving for \(F'\) gives the formula.

**Horizontal and vertical tangents.** The tangent is horizontal where \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 0\) and \(\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0\), and vertical where \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 0\) and \(\frac{dy}{dt} \ne 0\) (there the slope \(\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\) is unbounded, and the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swap: \(\frac{dx}{dy} = 0\)). Where both derivatives vanish, the formula gives no information and the point must be examined separately.

**Worked example.** Consider \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^3 - 3t\). Then \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\), \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3\), and
\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t}. \]
- *Horizontal tangents:* \(3t^2 - 3 = 0\) gives \(t = \pm1\), where \(2t \ne 0\): the points \((1, -2)\) and \((1, 2)\).
- *Vertical tangent:* \(2t = 0\) gives \(t = 0\), where \(\frac{dy}{dt} = -3 \ne 0\): the point \((0, 0)\).
- *A self-intersection:* \(x(t) = x(s)\) with \(t \ne s\) forces \(s = -t\), and then \(y(t) = y(-t)\) means \(t^3 - 3t = -(t^3 - 3t)\), so \(t^3 = 3t\), \(t = \pm\sqrt3\). Both values give the point \((3, 0)\). At \(t = \sqrt3\) the slope is \(\frac{9 - 3}{2\sqrt3} = \sqrt3\), and at \(t = -\sqrt3\) it is \(-\sqrt3\). The curve passes through \((3, 0)\) twice, with two different tangent lines, \(y = \sqrt3(x - 3)\) and \(y = -\sqrt3(x - 3)\).

```plot
x: -1, 5
y: -3, 3
t: -2.2, 2.2
param: t^2; t^3 - 3*t | x = t², y = t³ − 3t
f: sqrt(3)*(x - 3) | tangent at t = √3
f: -sqrt(3)*(x - 3) | tangent at t = −√3
point: 3, 0
point: 1, 2
point: 1, -2
point: 0, 0
```

A single equation \(y = F(x)\) could never produce two tangent lines at one point; the parametric description handles it naturally, because the two tangents belong to different values of \(t\).

**When both derivatives vanish: the cycloid's cusps.** For \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\), and at \(t = 2\pi\) both numerator and denominator are 0. The limits \(\lim_{t\to2\pi^-}\frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t} = -\infty\) and \(\lim_{t\to2\pi^+}\frac{\sin t}{1-\cos t} = +\infty\) show that the curve comes down steeply to the ground and leaves it steeply: a cusp with a vertical tangent direction.

**Common mistakes.** Inverting the quotient, \(\frac{dx/dt}{dy/dt}\), which is \(\frac{dx}{dy}\). Declaring a horizontal tangent wherever \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 0\) without checking \(\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0\). And giving a tangent line in terms of \(t\): the line must be written in \(x\) and \(y\), using the point \((x(t_0), y(t_0))\) and the numerical slope.

questions.prompt: For \(x = t^3 - 3t\), \(y = t^2\), find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) as a function of \(t\) (for \(t \ne \pm1\)).
questions.why: \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2t\) and \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 3t^2 - 3\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2t}{3t^2 - 3}\), defined where \(t \ne \pm1\) (those are the vertical tangents).

questions.prompt: For \(x = t^3 - 3t\), \(y = t^3 - 12t\), find all values of \(t\) at which the tangent line is horizontal.
questions.why: \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 3t^2 - 12 = 0\) gives \(t = \pm2\). At both, \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 3\cdot4 - 3 = 9 \ne 0\), so the tangents are genuinely horizontal. The points are \((2, -16)\) and \((-2, 16)\).

questions.prompt: Find the equation of the tangent line to \(x = 2\cos t\), \(y = 3\sin t\) at the point where \(t = \frac\pi4\). Give \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
questions.why: The point is \(\left(\sqrt2, \frac{3\sqrt2}{2}\right)\). The slope is \(\frac{3\cos t}{-2\sin t}\) at \(t = \frac\pi4\), i.e. \(-\frac32\). So \(y - \frac{3\sqrt2}{2} = -\frac32(x - \sqrt2)\), that is \(y = -\frac32x + 3\sqrt2\).

sections.title: The second derivative and concavity
sections.md:
Concavity of a graph is decided by the sign of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\). This section computes that second derivative for a parametric curve, a step that is often done incorrectly because the natural guess is wrong.

The slope \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) of a parametric curve is itself a function of \(t\); call it \(m(t) = \frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\). The second derivative is the derivative of \(m\) with respect to \(x\), and the argument of the previous section, applied to \(m\) in place of \(y\), gives
\[ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}, \qquad \text{where } \frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0. \]
Differentiate the slope with respect to \(t\), then divide by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\) once more.

**Worked example 1.** For \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^3 - 3t\), the slope is \(m(t) = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t} = \frac32\left(t - \frac1t\right)\). Then \(m'(t) = \frac32\left(1 + \frac{1}{t^2}\right) = \frac{3(t^2 + 1)}{2t^2}\), and dividing by \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t\),
\[ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3(t^2+1)}{4t^3}. \]
This is positive for \(t > 0\) and negative for \(t < 0\): the part of the curve traced for \(t > 0\) is concave up, and the part traced for \(t < 0\) is concave down. At the crossing point \((3, 0)\) the curve is concave up along one branch and concave down along the other, which again only a parametric description can express.

**Worked example 2 (the cycloid, \(r = 1\)).** Here \(m(t) = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\). By the quotient rule,
\[ m'(t) = \frac{\cos t\,(1 - \cos t) - \sin t\cdot\sin t}{(1 - \cos t)^2} = \frac{\cos t - 1}{(1-\cos t)^2} = -\frac{1}{1 - \cos t}, \]
and dividing by \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 1 - \cos t\) gives \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\frac{1}{(1 - \cos t)^2}\), which is negative wherever it is defined. Each arch of the cycloid is concave down, as the picture suggests.

**The tempting wrong formula.** It is not true that \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{y''(t)}{x''(t)}\). A decisive counterexample: \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^2\) for \(t > 0\) traces part of the line \(y = x\), whose second derivative is 0, while \(\frac{y''}{x''} = \frac22 = 1\). The error comes from treating \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) as a fraction of second differentials; the correct formula follows from the chain rule applied to the first derivative.

**Common mistakes.** Using \(\frac{y''}{x''}\), as just discussed. Forgetting the final division by \(\frac{dx}{dt}\), which gives \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\) instead of \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\). And reading concavity from the sign of \(m'(t)\) alone, which is wrong whenever \(\frac{dx}{dt} < 0\).

questions.prompt: For \(x = t^2 + 1\), \(y = t^3 - t\), find \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) as a function of \(t\) (\(t \ne 0\)).

A student computes \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) for a parametric curve as \(\frac{y''(t)}{x''(t)}\). Give a specific parametric curve for which this is wrong, and derive the correct formula from the chain rule.
rubric: Gives a counterexample, e.g. \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^2\) (\(t > 0\)): the line \(y = x\) has \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0\) but \(\frac{y''}{x''} = 1\).
Notes that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = m(t)\) is a function of \(t\).
Applies the chain rule \(\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{dm}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}\) to get \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{m'(t)}{x'(t)}\).
States the condition \(x'(t) \ne 0\).
questions.model: Counterexample: \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^2\), \(t > 0\), traces part of the line \(y = x\), so \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0\); but \(\frac{y''(t)}{x''(t)} = \frac22 = 1\). Correct formula: the slope \(m(t) = \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\) is a function of \(t\), and \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) is its derivative with respect to \(x\). Where \(x'(t) \ne 0\), \(m\) is a differentiable function of \(x\), and the chain rule gives \(\frac{dm}{dt} = \frac{dm}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}\). Hence \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{dm}{dx} = \frac{m'(t)}{x'(t)}\).
questions.why: The same chain-rule step that gives \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y'}{x'}\) is applied a second time, to the slope.

sections.title: Area under a parametric curve
sections.md:
The area under a graph \(y = F(x)\) is \(\int_a^b F(x)\,dx\). For a curve given parametrically, the same area can be computed without eliminating the parameter, by substituting \(x = x(t)\) in that integral. This section derives the resulting formula, explains the role of orientation, and extends it to regions enclosed by closed curves.

**The formula.** Suppose a curve \(x = x(t)\), \(y = y(t)\), \(\alpha \le t \le \beta\), is traced once from left to right (\(x'(t) > 0\)), with \(y(t) \ge 0\), and \(x'\) is continuous. The area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis is \(\int y\,dx\), and the substitution \(x = x(t)\), \(dx = x'(t)\,dt\) gives
\[ A = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta} y(t)\,x'(t)\,dt. \]
If instead the curve is traced from right to left (\(x'(t) < 0\)), the same integral equals \(-A\), because the substitution reverses the limits of \(x\). The integral records the direction of travel; the area is its absolute value in that case.

**Worked example 1 (one arch of the cycloid).** For \(x = r(t - \sin t)\), \(y = r(1 - \cos t)\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), the curve runs left to right with \(y \ge 0\), and \(x'(t) = r(1 - \cos t)\). So
\[ A = \int_0^{2\pi} r(1 - \cos t)\cdot r(1 - \cos t)\,dt = r^2\int_0^{2\pi}\left(1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t\right)dt = r^2(2\pi - 0 + \pi) = 3\pi r^2, \]
using \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2t\,dt = \pi\). The area under one arch is three times the area of the rolling wheel.

**Closed curves.** Let a simple closed curve (one that does not cross itself) be traced once counterclockwise as \(t\) runs from \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\), and suppose the region it encloses lies between an upper and a lower boundary curve. The upper boundary is then traced from right to left and its lower boundary from left to right. The integral \(\int_\alpha^\beta y\,x'\,dt\) therefore equals (minus the area under the upper boundary) plus (the area under the lower boundary), which is minus the enclosed area:
\[ A = -\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} y(t)\,x'(t)\,dt \qquad \text{(simple closed curve, counterclockwise)}. \]
The argument above assumed the region lies above the \(x\)-axis, but shifting the curve vertically changes \(y\) by a constant \(c\) and the integral by \(c\int_\alpha^\beta x'\,dt = c\,(x(\beta) - x(\alpha)) = 0\), so the formula holds in general.

**Worked example 2 (the ellipse).** For \(x = a\cos t\), \(y = b\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\) (counterclockwise),
\[ A = -\int_0^{2\pi} b\sin t\cdot(-a\sin t)\,dt = ab\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 t\,dt = \pi ab. \]
For \(a = b = r\) this is the area \(\pi r^2\) of the disc.

**Common mistakes.** Writing \(\int y(t)\,dt\), which omits the factor \(x'(t)\) coming from \(dx\). Putting \(x\)-values as the limits of a \(t\)-integral. And ignoring orientation, which produces a negative answer: \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\), \(0 \le t \le \pi\), traces the upper semicircle from right to left, and \(\int_0^\pi \sin t\,(-\sin t)\,dt = -\frac\pi2\), whereas the area is \(\frac\pi2\).

questions.prompt: Find the area under one arch of the cycloid \(x = 2(t - \sin t)\), \(y = 2(1 - \cos t)\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).
questions.why: \(A = \int_0^{2\pi} y\,x'\,dt = \int_0^{2\pi} 4(1 - \cos t)^2\,dt = 4\cdot 3\pi = 12\pi\), which is \(3\pi r^2\) with \(r = 2\).

questions.prompt: Find the area between the \(x\)-axis and the curve \(x = t^2 + 1\), \(y = t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\), using the parametric area formula.
questions.why: For \(0 \le t \le 2\), \(x' = 2t \ge 0\) (left to right) and \(y \ge 0\). \(A = \int_0^2 t\cdot2t\,dt = \frac{2t^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = \frac{16}{3}\). Check: the curve is \(y = \sqrt{x - 1}\), \(1 \le x \le 5\), and \(\int_1^5\sqrt{x-1}\,dx = \frac23\cdot4^{3/2} = \frac{16}3\).

sections.title: Arc length, speed and surface area
sections.md:
The last question of this chapter is how long a parametric curve is. The answer also gives the speed of a moving point, and, with one more factor, the area of a surface of revolution.

**Arc length.** Divide \([\alpha, \beta]\) into \(n\) pieces of width \(\Delta t\) and join the corresponding points of the curve by line segments. The \(i\)th segment has length \(\sqrt{(\Delta x_i)^2 + (\Delta y_i)^2}\), and by the mean value theorem \(\Delta x_i = x'(t_i^*)\Delta t\) and \(\Delta y_i = y'(t_i^{**})\Delta t\) for points \(t_i^*, t_i^{**}\) in the \(i\)th piece. The total length of the polygon is therefore close to the Riemann sum \(\sum\sqrt{x'(t_i)^2 + y'(t_i)^2}\,\Delta t\), and in the limit:

> **Arc length of a parametric curve.** If \(x'\) and \(y'\) are continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\) and the curve is traced exactly once as \(t\) increases from \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\), its length is
> \[ L = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt. \]

For a graph (\(x = t\), \(y = F(t)\)) this reduces to the familiar \(\int_a^b\sqrt{1 + F'(x)^2}\,dx\).

**Speed.** The length of the path from time \(\alpha\) to time \(t\) is \(s(t) = \int_\alpha^t\sqrt{x'(u)^2 + y'(u)^2}\,du\), and by the fundamental theorem of calculus
\[ \frac{ds}{dt} = \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}, \]
the rate at which distance along the path is covered: the **speed** of the moving point.

**Worked example 1 (circle).** For \(x = r\cos t\), \(y = r\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\): \(x'^2 + y'^2 = r^2\sin^2 t + r^2\cos^2 t = r^2\), so the speed is constant, \(r\), and \(L = 2\pi r\).

**Worked example 2 (cycloid).** For one arch, \(x' = r(1 - \cos t)\), \(y' = r\sin t\), so
\[ x'^2 + y'^2 = r^2\left(1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t\right) = 2r^2(1 - \cos t) = 4r^2\sin^2\tfrac t2. \]
On \([0, 2\pi]\), \(\sin\frac t2 \ge 0\), so the speed is \(2r\sin\frac t2\) and
\[ L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2r\sin\tfrac t2\,dt = \left[-4r\cos\tfrac t2\right]_0^{2\pi} = 8r. \]
The speed is 0 at the cusps, confirming that the rim point is momentarily at rest when it touches the ground.

**Why "traced exactly once" matters.** For \(x = \cos 2t\), \(y = \sin 2t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), the integral is \(\int_0^{2\pi} 2\,dt = 4\pi\): the distance travelled by a point that goes around the unit circle twice, not the length \(2\pi\) of the circle.

**Surface area.** Rotating about the \(x\)-axis a curve traced once with \(y(t) \ge 0\) sweeps out a surface whose area is
\[ S = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi\,y(t)\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt, \]
the parametric form of \(\int 2\pi y\,ds\): each small piece of length \(ds\) at height \(y\) sweeps a band of circumference \(2\pi y\). For the upper semicircle \(x = r\cos t\), \(y = r\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le \pi\), this gives \(\int_0^\pi 2\pi r\sin t\cdot r\,dt = 4\pi r^2\), the area of a sphere.

**Common mistakes.** Forgetting the square root, or squaring \(x' + y'\) instead of adding squares. Integrating over an interval on which the curve is traced more than once. And simplifying \(\sqrt{4r^2\sin^2\frac t2}\) to \(2r\sin\frac t2\) without checking the sign of \(\sin\frac t2\) on the interval.

questions.prompt: Find the length of the curve \(x = t^2\), \(y = \frac23t^3\), \(0 \le t \le \sqrt3\).
Find the length of one arch of the cycloid \(x = 3(t - \sin t)\), \(y = 3(1 - \cos t)\).
questions.why: \(x'^2 + y'^2 = 9\left[(1 - \cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t\right] = 18(1 - \cos t) = 36\sin^2\frac t2\). On \([0, 2\pi]\) the speed is \(6\sin\frac t2\), and \(L = \int_0^{2\pi}6\sin\frac t2\,dt = 24\), which is \(8r\) with \(r = 3\).

questions.prompt: A student computes the length of the unit circle from \(x = \cos 2t\), \(y = \sin 2t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), and obtains \(4\pi\). Explain what the integral actually measured, which hypothesis of the arc length formula was violated, and how to fix the computation.
rubric: Computes the speed \(\sqrt{4\sin^2 2t + 4\cos^2 2t} = 2\) and the integral \(4\pi\).
Explains that the integral is the distance travelled, and the point goes around the circle twice.
Identifies the violated hypothesis: the curve must be traced exactly once.
Fixes it: use \(0 \le t \le \pi\), giving \(2\pi\).
questions.model: Here \(x' = -2\sin 2t\), \(y' = 2\cos 2t\), so the speed is 2 and \(\int_0^{2\pi}2\,dt = 4\pi\). As \(t\) runs from 0 to \(2\pi\), the angle \(2t\) runs from 0 to \(4\pi\), so the point goes around the circle twice; the integral of speed is the total distance travelled, \(2\times2\pi\). The arc length formula requires that the curve be traced exactly once. Restricting to \(0 \le t \le \pi\) traces the circle once and gives \(\int_0^\pi 2\,dt = 2\pi\).
questions.why: Arc length is a property of the set of points; the integral of speed is a property of the motion. They agree only when each point is passed once.

terms.d: A pair of equations \(x = f(t)\), \(y = g(t)\) giving both coordinates as functions of a common variable \(t\).
The independent variable \(t\) in parametric equations, often interpreted as time.
The set of points \((f(t), g(t))\) as \(t\) ranges over an interval; also called a plane curve.
For \(a \le t \le b\), the points \((f(a), g(a))\) and \((f(b), g(b))\) where the tracing begins and ends.
The direction in which a parametric curve is traced as the parameter increases.
Deriving an equation in \(x\) and \(y\) alone from parametric equations, while keeping track of the restrictions the parametrization imposes.
A choice of parametric equations, with parameter interval, whose curve is a given set of points.
terms.ex: \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\) and \(x = \cos 2t\), \(y = \sin 2t\) parametrize the same circle differently.

terms.d: The path of a point on the rim of a wheel of radius \(r\) rolling without slipping along a line: \(x = r(t - \sin t)\), \(y = r(1 - \cos t)\).
A sharp point of a curve, where the direction of travel reverses abruptly; on the cycloid it occurs where \(x'(t) = y'(t) = 0\).
The rate \(\frac{ds}{dt} = \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\) at which arc length is covered by the moving point.

cards.back: The set of points \((f(t), g(t))\), \(t\) in an interval; \(t\) is the parameter.

cards.front: What information does a parametrization carry that the equation of its curve does not?
cards.back: Starting point, direction of travel (orientation), speed, and how many times the curve is traced.

cards.front: Eliminating the parameter in \(x = \sqrt t\), \(y = t\): what is easy to miss?
cards.back: The restriction \(x \ge 0\): the curve is only the right half of \(y = x^2\).
\(x = h + r\cos t\), \(y = k + r\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).

cards.front: Parametric equations of the cycloid (wheel radius \(r\))
Conditions for horizontal and vertical tangents of a parametric curve
cards.back: Horizontal: \(y' = 0\), \(x' \ne 0\). Vertical: \(x' = 0\), \(y' \ne 0\). Both 0: examine separately (e.g. a cusp).

cards.front: How can a parametric curve have two tangent lines at one point?
cards.back: It passes through the point at two different values of \(t\), with a different slope at each.

cards.front: Area under a parametric curve traced left to right
cards.back: \(A = \int_\alpha^\beta y(t)\,x'(t)\,dt\) (the integral is negative if traced right to left).

cards.front: Area inside a simple closed curve traced counterclockwise
Arc length of a parametric curve
What does \(\int\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}\,dt\) measure if the curve is traced twice?
cards.back: The distance travelled, which is twice the arc length.

cards.front: Surface area: parametric curve rotated about the \(x\)-axis
Area under one arch of a cycloid with \(r = 1\)
Length of one arch of a cycloid with \(r = 1\)
Speed of a point moving along \((x(t), y(t))\)

practice.prompt: Eliminate the parameter from \(x = e^t\), \(y = e^{2t} + 1\), giving \(y\) as a function of \(x\). (State the restriction on \(x\) in your working.)
practice.why: \(e^{2t} = (e^t)^2 = x^2\), so \(y = x^2 + 1\). Since \(x = e^t > 0\), the curve is only the part of the parabola with \(x > 0\).

practice.prompt: Parametrize the circle with centre \((2, -1)\) and radius 3, traced once clockwise starting at \((5, -1)\). Verify both the starting point and the direction.
rubric: Gives \(x = 2 + 3\cos t\), \(y = -1 - 3\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\) (or equivalent).
Checks \(t = 0\) gives \((5, -1)\).
Shows the direction is clockwise, e.g. \(y\) decreases for small \(t > 0\) while \(x\) decreases.
practice.model: Take \(x = 2 + 3\cos t\), \(y = -1 - 3\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\). Then \((x-2)^2 + (y+1)^2 = 9\cos^2t + 9\sin^2t = 9\), so every point is on the circle. At \(t = 0\) the point is \((5, -1)\). For small \(t > 0\), \(y = -1 - 3\sin t < -1\): the point moves from the rightmost point downward, which is clockwise. At \(t = \frac\pi2\) it is at \((2, -4)\), the bottom, confirming the direction.
practice.why: Negating the sine term reverses the direction of travel.

practice.prompt: For the cycloid \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\), find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) as a function of \(t\).
practice.why: \(\frac{dy}{dt} = \sin t\), \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 1 - \cos t\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\), defined for \(t \ne 2\pi k\).

practice.prompt: Find the slope of the tangent to the cycloid \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\) at \(t = \frac\pi3\).
For \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin 2t\), \(0 \le t < 2\pi\), find all points where the tangent line is horizontal and all points where it is vertical.
rubric: Horizontal: \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos 2t = 0\) gives \(t = \frac\pi4, \frac{3\pi}4, \frac{5\pi}4, \frac{7\pi}4\), where \(\frac{dx}{dt} = -\sin t \ne 0\).
Lists the points \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2, 1\right), \left(-\frac{\sqrt2}2, -1\right), \left(-\frac{\sqrt2}2, 1\right), \left(\frac{\sqrt2}2, -1\right)\).
Vertical: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = 0\) at \(t = 0, \pi\), where \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2 \ne 0\): points \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\).
practice.model: \(\frac{dx}{dt} = -\sin t\), \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos 2t\). Horizontal tangents: \(\cos 2t = 0\), so \(2t = \frac\pi2 + k\pi\), \(t = \frac\pi4, \frac{3\pi}4, \frac{5\pi}4, \frac{7\pi}4\) in \([0, 2\pi)\). At these \(\sin t \ne 0\), so the tangents are horizontal, at \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, 1\right)\), \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, -1\right)\), \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, 1\right)\), \(\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}, -1\right)\) respectively. Vertical tangents: \(\sin t = 0\), \(t = 0, \pi\), where \(\frac{dy}{dt} = 2\cos 0 = 2\) and \(2\cos 2\pi = 2\), both nonzero; the points are \((1, 0)\) and \((-1, 0)\).
practice.why: The curve is a figure-eight (a Lissajous curve) passing through the origin twice, at \(t = \frac\pi2\) and \(t = \frac{3\pi}{2}\).

practice.prompt: For \(x = t^2 + 1\), \(y = t^3 - t\), find the value of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\) at \(t = 1\).
practice.why: From \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3t^2 + 1}{4t^3}\) (differentiate \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 1}{2t}\) with respect to \(t\) and divide by \(2t\)), at \(t = 1\) the value is \(\frac{4}{4} = 1\).

practice.prompt: Find the area enclosed by the astroid \(x = \cos^3 t\), \(y = \sin^3 t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\) (traced counterclockwise).
Find the total length of the astroid \(x = \cos^3 t\), \(y = \sin^3 t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\).
practice.why: \(x'^2 + y'^2 = 9\cos^4t\sin^2t + 9\sin^4t\cos^2t = 9\sin^2t\cos^2t\), so the speed is \(3|\sin t\cos t|\). By symmetry, \(L = 4\int_0^{\pi/2}3\sin t\cos t\,dt = 4\cdot\frac32 = 6\). The absolute value matters: integrating \(3\sin t\cos t\) over \([0, 2\pi]\) would give 0.

practice.prompt: Rotate the curve \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\), \(0 \le t \le \pi\) about the \(x\)-axis. Use the parametric surface area formula to find the area of the resulting surface.
practice.why: The speed is 1 and \(y = \sin t \ge 0\), so \(S = \int_0^\pi 2\pi\sin t\,dt = 4\pi\), the area of the unit sphere.

practice.prompt: A particle moves along \(x = 3t\), \(y = 4t - t^2\). Find its minimum speed.
practice.why: Speed \(= \sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2} = \sqrt{9 + (4 - 2t)^2}\), which is smallest when \(4 - 2t = 0\), i.e. \(t = 2\), where it equals 3. At that instant the particle is at the top of its parabolic path, moving horizontally.

practice.prompt: For a parametric curve with \(x'(t) \ne 0\), which expression equals \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\)?
practice.why: Differentiate the slope \(\frac{y'}{x'}\) with respect to \(t\), then divide by \(x'(t)\). Option 1 is the tempting fraction of second derivatives, false for \(x = y = t^2\). Option 3, \(\frac{d}{dt}\) of the slope, omits the final division by \(x'(t)\), and option 4 multiplies by \(x'(t)\) where the chain rule requires dividing.

practice.prompt: Compute \(\int_0^\pi y(t)\,x'(t)\,dt\) for \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\). Explain why the result is negative, and give the area of the region between this curve and the \(x\)-axis.
rubric: Computes \(\int_0^\pi\sin t(-\sin t)\,dt = -\frac\pi2\).
Explains that \(x = \cos t\) decreases on \([0, \pi]\): the curve is traced right to left.
Explains that the substitution \(x = \cos t\) turns \(\int_{-1}^{1}y\,dx\) into an integral from \(t = \pi\) to \(t = 0\), so integrating from 0 to \(\pi\) gives the negative.
States the area \(\frac\pi2\).
practice.model: \(\int_0^\pi \sin t\cdot(-\sin t)\,dt = -\int_0^\pi\sin^2t\,dt = -\frac\pi2\). The curve is the upper unit semicircle, traced from \((1, 0)\) to \((-1, 0)\) as \(t\) goes from 0 to \(\pi\): right to left, since \(x' = -\sin t < 0\). The area is \(\int_{-1}^{1}y\,dx\); under \(x = \cos t\), \(x = -1\) corresponds to \(t = \pi\) and \(x = 1\) to \(t = 0\), so the area equals \(\int_\pi^0 y\,x'\,dt = +\frac\pi2\). Integrating in the direction of increasing \(t\) reverses the limits and the sign. The area is \(\frac\pi2\).
practice.why: The integral \(\int y\,x'\,dt\) is a signed quantity that records the direction of travel.

exam.prompt: For the curve \(x = t^2\), \(y = t^3 - 3t\): (a) find the points with horizontal and with vertical tangent lines; (b) show that the curve passes through \((3, 0)\) twice and find the equations of both tangent lines there; (c) determine where the curve is concave up and where concave down, in terms of \(t\).
rubric: (a) Horizontal at \(t = \pm1\): \((1, -2)\), \((1, 2)\); vertical at \(t = 0\): \((0, 0)\), with the nonvanishing of the other derivative checked.
(b) Shows \(t = \pm\sqrt3\) both give \((3, 0)\) and computes slopes \(\pm\sqrt3\).
(b) Tangent lines \(y = \sqrt3(x - 3)\) and \(y = -\sqrt3(x-3)\).
(c) \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3(t^2+1)}{4t^3}\): concave up for \(t > 0\), concave down for \(t < 0\).
exam.model: \(x' = 2t\), \(y' = 3t^2 - 3\), \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2 - 3}{2t}\). (a) \(y' = 0\) at \(t = \pm1\), where \(x' = \pm2 \ne 0\): horizontal tangents at \((1, -2)\) (\(t = 1\)) and \((1, 2)\) (\(t = -1\)). \(x' = 0\) at \(t = 0\), where \(y' = -3 \ne 0\): vertical tangent at \((0, 0)\). (b) At \(t = \sqrt3\): \(x = 3\), \(y = 3\sqrt3 - 3\sqrt3 = 0\); at \(t = -\sqrt3\): \(x = 3\), \(y = -3\sqrt3 + 3\sqrt3 = 0\). Slopes: \(\frac{9 - 3}{\pm2\sqrt3} = \pm\sqrt3\). Tangent lines: \(y = \sqrt3(x-3)\) and \(y = -\sqrt3(x - 3)\). (c) \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac32\left(t - \frac1t\right)\right) = \frac32\left(1 + \frac1{t^2}\right)\); dividing by \(2t\), \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3(t^2+1)}{4t^3}\), positive for \(t > 0\) (concave up) and negative for \(t < 0\) (concave down).
exam.why: A complete analysis of a parametric curve: slope, special tangents, self-intersection and concavity.

exam.prompt: Find the length of the curve \(x = e^t\cos t\), \(y = e^t\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le \ln 2\).
exam.why: \(x' = e^t(\cos t - \sin t)\), \(y' = e^t(\sin t + \cos t)\), so \(x'^2 + y'^2 = e^{2t}\left[(\cos t - \sin t)^2 + (\sin t + \cos t)^2\right] = 2e^{2t}\). The speed is \(\sqrt2e^t\) and \(L = \sqrt2\int_0^{\ln2}e^t\,dt = \sqrt2(2 - 1) = \sqrt2\).

exam.prompt: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse \(x = 4\cos t\), \(y = 3\sin t\), \(0 \le t \le 2\pi\), using a parametric area integral.
exam.why: The ellipse is traced counterclockwise, so \(A = -\int_0^{2\pi}3\sin t\cdot(-4\sin t)\,dt = 12\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2t\,dt = 12\pi\), which is \(\pi ab\) with \(a = 4\), \(b = 3\).

exam.prompt: Find the equation of the tangent line to \(x = t^2 + t\), \(y = t^2 - t\) at \(t = 1\). Give \(y\) as a function of \(x\).
exam.why: At \(t = 1\) the point is \((2, 0)\). \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{2t - 1}{2t + 1} = \frac13\) at \(t = 1\). So \(y = \frac13(x - 2)\).

exam.prompt: Derive the formula \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\), stating the hypothesis it needs. Then explain what happens on the cycloid \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\) at \(t = 2\pi\), where both derivatives are 0, by computing one-sided limits of the slope.
rubric: Hypothesis: \(x'(t) \ne 0\) (with \(x'\) continuous) so that \(y\) is locally a differentiable function of \(x\).
Chain rule: \(y'(t) = \frac{dy}{dx}\,x'(t)\), then divides by \(x'(t)\).
Cycloid slope \(\frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\), a \(\frac00\) form at \(2\pi\).
One-sided limits \(-\infty\) (from the left) and \(+\infty\) (from the right): a cusp with vertical tangent direction.
exam.model: If \(x'\) is continuous and \(x'(t_0) \ne 0\), then \(x\) is strictly monotone near \(t_0\), so near that point the curve is the graph of a function \(y = F(x)\), differentiable by the inverse function theorem. Differentiating \(y(t) = F(x(t))\) gives \(y'(t) = F'(x(t))\,x'(t)\), so \(\frac{dy}{dx} = F'(x) = \frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}\). For the cycloid, \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\), and at \(t = 2\pi\) both \(\sin t\) and \(1 - \cos t\) vanish, so the hypothesis fails. Near \(2\pi\), \(\sin t \approx t - 2\pi\) and \(1 - \cos t \approx \frac{(t - 2\pi)^2}{2}\), so the slope is approximately \(\frac{2}{t - 2\pi}\), which tends to \(-\infty\) as \(t \to 2\pi^-\) and to \(+\infty\) as \(t \to 2\pi^+\). The curve descends to the ground vertically and rises from it vertically: a cusp.
exam.why: When \(x' = y' = 0\) the moving point is momentarily at rest, and the curve can have a sharp point there even though both coordinate functions are smooth.

rules.name: Eliminate the parameter
rules.formula: Solve for \(t\) or use an identity such as \(\cos^2t + \sin^2t = 1\)
rules.watch: Keep the restrictions from the ranges of x(t) and y(t).

rules.name: Standard parametrizations
rules.formula: Segment \(P_0 + t(P_1 - P_0)\); circle \((h + r\cos t, k + r\sin t)\)
rules.watch: Check the start point and the direction.

rules.name: Slope
rules.when: Tangent lines, horizontal and vertical tangents.

rules.name: Area under a curve
rules.when: Curve traced once left to right above the axis.

rules.name: Enclosed area
rules.watch: The curve must not cross itself and must be traced once.

rules.name: Arc length
rules.when: Length of a path traced once; distance travelled in general.

rules.name: Surface area
rules.watch: Rotation about the y-axis uses x in place of y.

stuck: Make a table of \(t\), \(x\), \(y\) for five or six values of \(t\) to see the shape and the orientation.
For special tangents, solve \(x'(t) = 0\) and \(y'(t) = 0\) separately, then check the other derivative at each solution.
To find where a curve crosses itself, solve \(x(t) = x(s)\), \(y(t) = y(s)\) with \(t \ne s\).
For areas and lengths, write everything in \(t\), including the limits, before integrating.
Simplify \(x'^2 + y'^2\) with identities (\(\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1\), \(1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2\frac t2\)) before taking the square root.
